planting.note: Container or balled-and-burlapped stock establishes best when planted in cool fall weather with consistent soil moisture.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet soil along streambanks, pond edges, or low-lying ground where few other large trees tolerate standing water. The roots fix nitrogen via symbiotic bacteria, so this species thrives in poor, boggy sites and improves soil fertility over time. Prune only to remove damaged wood, since the naturally pyramidal form needs little shaping. Watch for alder leaf beetle and occasional canker in stressed trees, but overall this is a tough, fast-establishing pioneer tree.

planting.note: Best transplanted while dormant into moist, well-drained soil near streams or seasonally wet lowland sites.

directions: This fast-growing Pacific Northwest native colonizes disturbed, moist ground and riparian corridors, where its nitrogen-fixing roots rebuild fertility after logging or flooding. Give it full sun and reliable moisture; it struggles in dry upland soils and short-lived trees often decline after 60-100 years. Catkins appear before the leaves in late winter, providing early pollen for emerging insects. Use it for erosion control on streambanks or as a quick-canopy pioneer species rather than a long-term specimen tree.

planting.note: Tolerant of dry sites compared to other alders; plant balled stock in fall or early spring in any reasonably fertile soil.

directions: Unlike most alders, this southern Italian and Corsican native handles ordinary garden soil and even brief dry spells once established, making it a practical fast-growing street or screen tree outside wetland settings. Glossy, heart-shaped leaves stay attractive well into autumn, and showy pendulous catkins open in late winter before leaf-out. Its pyramidal habit and tolerance of pollution and compacted soil suit urban plantings. Stake young trees in windy sites until the root system anchors.
sources: Bean's Trees and Shrubs Hardy in the British Isles

planting.note: Plant balled or container stock in deep, fertile soil; avoid sites with heavy Dutch elm disease pressure unless resistant selections are preferred.

directions: This broad-crowned European and western Asian elm tolerates cool, moist climates and shaded woodland edges better than most elms, seeding itself readily where conditions suit. Its large, rough-surfaced leaves and relatively short samara-to-seedling cycle make it among the fastest elms to naturalize in hedgerows and riparian woods. Like other elms it remains vulnerable to Dutch elm disease, so monitor for wilting branches and consult regional extension guidance before planting at scale. Grows well in part shade when young, then needs full sun to develop its mature spreading canopy.
sources: Bean's Trees and Shrubs Hardy in the British Isles

planting.note: Plant container or balled stock in well-drained soil; tolerates lime and urban heat better than most ash species.

directions: Unlike the wind-pollinated flowers of most ash species, this small Mediterranean tree produces fragrant creamy-white panicles in late spring that draw bees and other pollinators, making it a genuine flowering shade tree for small gardens. It handles alkaline, rocky, and drought-prone soils with ease and holds up well as a street or courtyard tree in hot urban settings. Prune to a single leader while young to establish a tidy rounded crown. Give it full sun for the heaviest bloom display.
sources: Bean's Trees and Shrubs Hardy in the British Isles

planting.note: Establishes readily in heavy, seasonally wet floodplain soils across southern Europe; plant dormant stock in fall where winters are mild.

directions: This southern European and North African relative of common ash carries finer, narrower leaflets and a more open, airy crown than its northern counterpart, giving dappled rather than dense shade. It tolerates periodic flooding and heavy clay along river floodplains better than most other ash species, making it useful for riparian restoration or large park plantings in warmer zones. Provide full sun and consistent moisture while young. As with all ash, monitor regionally for emerald ash borer before planting at scale.
sources: Bean's Trees and Shrubs Hardy in the British Isles
